input.rationale: CheckRun 0e5183701ac3447c8398f246b9103a04 returned completed/tests_passed with exit 0, 17 parsed CA_EVENT observations and 0 parsing errors; indices 0-15 reproduce probes A-C unchanged and index 16 is the first sweep summary whose liveness counters are interpretable: seeds=60, steps_per_seed=60, elections=470, ordinary proposals=461, conf_change_proposals=262, restarts=429, unapplied_conf_change_states=48, stalled_states=0, violations=0. Because the antecedent now holds at 48 check points, the witness's zero is informative for this event set, and the receipt contains no liveness_witness event because the witness never fired. I interpret that, resolve the liveness half of the gap to the extent the receipt supports, and keep both halves scoped; no experiment is requested this turn.

interpretations.rationale: Index 16 gives the first sweep receipt in which the liveness witness has its antecedent and the safety counters are unchanged: application lag was introduced by skipping a randomly chosen node's apply step about one time in six, so 48 of the 3600 check points had at least one node holding a committed-but-unapplied configuration change, and in every one of those 48 states at least one node remained promotable - stalled_states=0 with no liveness_witness event emitted, since the witness only emits when the conjunction holds. That is a real, if descriptive, answer to the bounded-liveness question the guard raises: in this event set the campaign suppression never coincided with a configuration that had no candidate able to campaign, so the guard's cost never became a leaderless configuration here. The safety half is unchanged and now carries application lag as well: 262 configuration changes (half joint, with the target's own auto-leave), 429 restarts rebuilt from persisted state, 470 elections and 461 ordinary proposals produced violations=0, so no witness for at-most-one-leader-per-term, committed (index, term) consistency, committed-index monotonicity or applied<=committed. Both halves stay scoped: 48 antecedent observations over one fixed seed set bound nothing outside it, the witness is evaluated only at check points between events, and the event mix fixes how often lag and configuration changes overlap.

984747de5ed94b4ea8f6977b2a92808f-gap-2.explanation: The event-set items the gap named are covered by receipts: simple and joint configuration changes with the target's auto-leave and a real joining participant (CheckRuns 2a3cfe42597e4c9f813117a4f06d4bf1, ccc93c67a2b54e7a874ab9bc7eedce9a), restarts that rebuild a node from the persisted hard state and applied ConfState (c6015a9dcbe94734bfc7089fff19e5c1), and now application lag giving the liveness witness its antecedent (0e5183701ac3447c8398f246b9103a04 index 16: unapplied_conf_change_states=48, stalled_states=0). Within those event sets the four safety invariants held and the guard never left a configuration without a promotable node while a configuration change was pending.

knowledge.assertion: the witness's zero count is uninformative until the antecedent holds
application lag is what leaves a committed configuration change unapplied at a node

counterevidence: 48 antecedent observations out of 3600 check points is a thin sample for a liveness claim, and the sample is determined by the harness's own probability of skipping an apply step.
The witness checks promotability of any node, not whether a quorum of voters could actually campaign; a state where only a single node could campaign would still count as not stalled.
Demotion of an existing serving voter is still absent from the configuration events, and storage faults remain outside the event set.
limitations: The lag is one-step and random; sustained application stalls, or lag combined with a partition of the applied-lagging node, were not exercised.
Counts are descriptive; no rate or bound follows for other seeds, event mixes or cluster sizes.
Checks still occur between events, and committed entries are compared by term at an index rather than full identity.

interpretations.rationale: Source-only reading of the count-based read-only flow. Positive part: positions are monotonically increasing counts (never reused for a later batch), acks are maxima, and a released read carries the commit index recorded at admission, so a confirmed read cannot be justified by acknowledgements collected for an earlier request; the leader's own ack is the admission position, so a majority echo is still required for confirmation, and pendingReadIndexMessages are answered only after the leader commits in its term, which can only raise the emitted index. Unresolved part: the term-change path. reset() replaces r.readOnly with a fresh instance (unconfirmed reads and acks dropped) while r.readStates is untouched, and releasePendingReadIndexMessages only replies when committedEntryInCurrentTerm() holds. I have not yet observed whether a read admitted just before a term change is dropped silently (a lost completion under a legal trigger) or answered later; the snapshot's own TestReadOnlyDuplicateRequest covers only the duplicate-ctx/delayed-heartbeat case and asserts indices are not too small, not that every admitted request completes.
counterevidence: The repo's own read-index selections (TestReadOnlyOptionSafe/Lease/WithLearner/ForNewLeader/DuplicateRequest, TestRaftFreesReadOnlyMem) pass in native local feedback, and TestReadOnlyDuplicateRequest explicitly asserts no too-small read index under delayed duplicate requests plus a leader change, which weakens the stale-index side of the suspicion.
limitations: No retained execution receipt yet: the local test runs are construction feedback and cannot establish a formal conclusion.

Doc.go's Ready/Advance contract does not state that every admitted ReadIndex request must be answered, so a dropped request would have to be argued as a bounded-liveness consequence of an actual trigger rather than a contract violation.

interpretations.rationale: Source-only reading of the campaign admission guard. hasUnappliedConfChanges scans (applied, committed] with pagination and returns true on the first conf-change entry; hup() then refuses to campaign, and promotable() independently refuses while a snapshot is pending/unstable. The guard is consistent with doc.go's statement that configurations take effect when applied, and with applyConfChange/switchToConfig which only reconfigure on application, so a node that campaigns while lagging application would otherwise campaign with a stale voter set. What remains open is whether the guard is complete for the paths that can present a stale voter set (restore from snapshot with only ConfState initialized, bootstrap with applied<committed, an application that rejects a change by zeroing NodeId, and MsgTimeoutNow where the guard also suppresses a requested transfer), and whether the suppression can be permanent for an otherwise eligible voter.
limitations: No existing test references hasUnappliedConfChanges directly, so its behavior is currently only read from source; it must be probed with a real log/apply prefix rather than asserted.

interpretations.rationale: The suspicion had two branches: (i) the guard may be bypassed so a node campaigns with a stale voter set, and (ii) the guard may permanently block a legal campaign. Branch (i) is refuted by events 1 and 2: with has_unapplied=true and an already-promotable voter, both the MsgHup path and the MsgTimeoutNow path leave the node in StateFollower(term=1) with msgs=0, and the runner log shows the same suppression reason on both paths, so the transfer path reaches campaign() only through the same guard. The voter set used when campaigning is legitimate rather than stale: after the application catches up (event 3) the node reports has_unapplied=false and campaigns at term 2 with vote=1 and MsgVote addressed to voters [2,3], and event 0 records that this config (voters_before=[1,2,3]) is the applied configuration. Branch (ii) is refuted by the same event 3 plus the control at events 4-5: the block is transient, keyed on the entry type in (applied, committed] rather than on the applied/committed gap itself (the control has the identical gap and campaigns immediately). What remains is a bounded-liveness cost, not a safety defect: while the entry is unapplied the node cannot campaign and cannot take over a requested transfer, which is the documented intent that configurations take effect on application.

c6f44be10c0445b7a091b7db545cd614-gap-1.explanation: With a committed-but-unapplied conf change the node refrains from campaigning on both triggers (events 1-2: StateFollower, term 1, msgs=0; runner log 'cannot campaign at term 1 since there are still pending configuration changes to apply' on the MsgHup and MsgTimeoutNow paths), and a later campaign is possible once raft's applied index covers the entry (event 3: has_unapplied=false, StateCandidate at term 2, MsgVote to voters [2,3]; control events 4-5 show the effect is caused by the entry type, not by the applied/committed gap).

knowledge.assertion: hup() returns without campaigning when hasUnappliedConfChanges() is true, for both MsgHup and MsgTimeoutNow
campaign() addresses vote requests to the tracked voters of the current configuration, here [2,3]

counterevidence: The node is promotable=true throughout (events 0, 4), so the refusal does not come from promotable(); it is specifically hasUnappliedConfChanges, which strengthens the reading that the guard is the cause rather than an admission in promotable.

The post-apply campaign (event 3) carries vote targets [2,3] from the pre-change configuration because the harness only advanced raftLog.applied without calling ApplyConfChange; the voter set used in the probe is therefore the stored config, which is the config a leader would legitimately campaign with at that point.
limitations: The probe drives MsgHup/MsgTimeoutNow directly on a node whose storage prefix and Config.Applied are supplied, not a tick-driven election of a live cluster, so it establishes the guard's effect and its transience but not the wall-clock or tick cost of the suppression inside a running cluster.

The bounded-liveness cost for a requested transfer (leader keeps dropping proposals while leadTransferee != None) is visible in source but was not exercised by this harness; it is registered as investigation @transfer_stall.

interpretations.rationale: The question had two possible defect shapes: a stale (too small) read index, or a lost completion. Events 6-9 select the second and exclude the first for the exercised path. Event 7 shows the request admitted with unconfirmed_reads=1, read_states=0 and the admission commit index recorded as 2; event 8 shows that after the term change the node holds read_states=0, unconfirmed_reads=0, confirmed_reads=0 and ctx_A_completed=false, so the request is dropped, never emitted with a smaller index. Event 9 is the control that separates 'drops on term change' from 'read confirmation is broken': a read admitted on the new leader (commit_now=3, index_B=3) goes from read_states_before_ack=0 to read_states_after_ack=1 with ctx_B_completed=true as soon as one peer heartbeat response carrying the leader's context arrives, which is also the count-based confirmation the source predicted. A dropped completion is not a defect under the applicable contract: Node.ReadIndex documents that the request can be lost without notice and that ensuring read index retries is the user's job, so the caller duty is established by the target's own interface statement, and the exercised drop is exactly that documented lossiness rather than a wrong index being served.

c6f44be10c0445b7a091b7db545cd614-gap-0.explanation: The request is dropped, not answered stale: after admission with unconfirmed_reads=1 (event 7), the term change leaves read_states=0, unconfirmed_reads=0, confirmed_reads=0 and ctx_A_completed=false (event 8), so nothing is emitted for that context and no smaller index can be observed; the confirmation path itself still functions on the new leader (event 9: ctx_B_completed=true with index_B=3 equal to the commit index at admission), and the lossiness is the caller duty stated by Node.ReadIndex.

knowledge.assertion: a released ReadState is justified by a quorum of ack positions and carries the commit index recorded at admission

limitations: The probe steps MsgReadIndex directly into the leader rather than through Node.ReadIndex/RawNode.ReadIndex, so it shows the state-machine outcome and not the API-level return value or the Ready/ReadStates plumbing; the documented caller duty was read from node.go/doc.go rather than exercised.

Only one trigger of the term change was exercised (a higher-term campaign message from a peer); other authority losses that rebuild readOnly (for example a snapshot restore or a leadership transfer racing an admitted read) were not covered.
interpretations.joint_history: Same single invocation as the campaign-admission interpretation: CheckRun 238d3a23d8624c438b85ec18f90a7b2b is one execution of one fixed harness (fixed-experiments/075c21493fd94adc9bdc30a30b2cbff1-experiment/assurance_generated_test.go) containing both probes, so events 6-9 and events 0-5 come from the same process, the same fixed inputs and the same receipt, with no separate producer or intermediate history between them. The experiment record is attached to question-1 because the submission can carry only one experiment request; the receipt itself is shared, and its parsed indices 6-9 are the decisive operands for this question.

interpretations.rationale: The declared hypothesis was that the transfer neither completes nor deadlocks but is bounded by one election timeout, with proposals resuming afterwards and the transfer becoming possible once the transferee applies its committed configuration. The receipt confirms each leg in order. Event 10 establishes the prefix the claim needs: the leader is StateLeader(term 1, committed 2), the transferee is StateFollower with applied 0 and committed 2 and has_unapplied true, and the leader already has the transferee matched to its last index (r1_match_r2 2 == r1_last_index 2), which is exactly the condition under which the leader sends MsgTimeoutNow immediately. Event 11 shows the transfer is accepted as a pending duty (lead_transferee 2) while the transferee does not campaign (StateFollower, term 1), so the guard is what stops the handover rather than a transport or match problem. Event 12 shows the cost is real but scoped: a proposal during the window returns 'raft proposal dropped' (is_proposal_dropped true). Event 13 shows the bound: after the leader's electionTimeout ticks, lead_transferee is 0, the leader is still StateLeader(term 1) and a proposal is accepted again (proposal_err empty), i.e. abortLeaderTransfer released the pending duty within one election timeout instead of leaving it forever pending. Events 14-15 show the duty is transferable rather than lost: once the transferee's applied index reaches its committed index (has_unapplied false), the retried transfer completes with the transferee as StateLeader(term 2) and the former leader as StateFollower(term 2). A delayed transfer whose delay is caused by the transferee's own application lag, with the old leader still able to serve proposals after the abort, is not a defect under the stated conditions; the honest counterweight is that during the window the leader rejects client proposals, which is a client-visible cost of a request the application itself asked for, and the sweep of random configurations and authority changes remains to be done.

knowledge.assertion: hup() refuses to campaign on the leadership-transfer path reached via MsgTimeoutNow while hasUnappliedConfChanges() is true
campaign() addresses vote requests only to the tracked voters of the current configuration, as in the completed retry at term 2

counterevidence: Event 12 shows a proposal is rejected with ErrProposalDropped while the transfer is pending, so the bounded-liveness account must not be read as 'no cost': the cost is a proposal-rejection window whose length is determined by the transferee's application lag, and the receipt only measures it for one tick-driven abort (event 13) rather than for a live cluster's scheduling.

Events 10-15 exercise one configuration (three voters plus a staged learner) and one transfer target; nothing in the receipt constrains the same sequence during a joint configuration or when the transferee is the only node lagging while the rest are applied.
limitations: Application lag is modelled by not advancing raftLog.applied on the transferee; the receipt therefore shows the protocol's behavior given that lag, not how a real application creates it.
The abort was produced by ticking the leader through its own electionTimeout, so the bound observed is in protocol ticks under this harness's scheduling rather than wall-clock time.

The transfer completes in the receipt through the network's MsgTimeoutNow delivery on the retry; no independent completion path (for example a transfer while the leader is also being removed) was exercised.

interpretations.rationale: Index 16 reports the sweep's only output: 60 seeds times 60 steps produced 459 elections and 446 proposals with violations=0, and the event carries the note that absence of violations is a holds-only result for this event set rather than a safety proof. For the four invariants actually checked after every event - at most one leader per term, no index already known committed ever observed with a different term, per-node committed-index monotonicity, and applied <= committed - the receipt therefore contains no counterexample, which is consistent with the source-level explanation that commitment and leadership require quorum-intersecting support under the simple configuration used here (MajorityConfig.CommittedIndex/VoteResult with the joint min/majority semantics). The absence is nevertheless bounded by what the harness actually did: it emitted no violation event of any of the four kinds, and it also emitted no configuration-change or restart event, because the executed case omits both while the registered discriminator named them. I am recording that as a necessary gap and keeping the conclusion scoped to the exercised event set; the defect claim is refuted only in the narrow sense that this event set produced no witness for the suspicion, not because the invariants were established for the protocol.
counterevidence: The sweep's coverage is smaller than the discriminator promised: no ConfChange/ConfChangeV2 proposal, no joint or learner configuration and no restart from persisted storage appeared in the event stream, so the mechanism most likely to threaten the invariants (support counted under a configuration that changes while entries are unapplied) was not part of this receipt.

A zero-violation count over 60 seeds cannot bound the violation rate; it states only that no witness appeared in this fixed event set, and the harness checked committed terms only for indices the nodes actually reported as committed, so an entry committed by a majority but never observed at any checked node is invisible to it.
limitations: Invariant checking happens after each event, not during message delivery, so an intermediate inconsistency that is repaired before the next check point would not be observed.
The committed-entry check compares terms at an index rather than full entry identity, which is adequate for log-matching violations but does not by itself detect a same-term payload difference.
Application is modelled with nextEnts on every step, so the applied index is never more than one event behind committed; a real application's lag patterns are not represented.
No comparison or requirement anchors were declared for this case in the experiment request, so the receipt carries parsed events only and its meaning rests on this interpretation.

interpretations.rationale: Index 16 shows the sweep with configuration changes admitted into the event stream: 317 conf-change proposals were actually issued (against 452 ordinary proposals and 467 elections) and the four invariants still reported violations=0, so the receipt contains no witness for at-most-one-leader-per-term, committed (index, term) divergence, committed-index regression, or applied > committed once nodes apply committed conf changes through applyConfChange. This is the first receipt whose event set reaches the mechanism the suspicion named - support counted while the tracked configuration changes - because the earlier revision applied no configuration at all. The absence is still bounded: the changes are single-node Changes on node 4 only, so no joint configuration and no promotion/demotion of an existing voter was exercised, node 4 never responded (black-hole stepper) so every committed decision rested on the original three voters, and restarts from persisted storage are missing entirely. Two construction facts from this revision belong in the record: messages addressed to a configured-but-absent node crash the repository's network helper (raft_test.go:4117 dereferences a missing state machine), and only registering the package's own black-hole stepper for that id makes configuration events safe to run; consequently the receipt's configuration coverage is real but does not include a newly configured node that participates. The conclusion is therefore holds-only for this event set, with the defect claim refuted only in the narrow sense that no witness appeared.
counterevidence: Only single-node changes on node 4 were proposed, so the joint-consensus decision path (both halves of a joint quorum) was not part of the event stream even though the gap names it.
Node 4 never processed a message, so configuration changes altered quorums and progress tracking without ever testing whether a freshly added participant can vote, be promoted, or be snapshotted.

The sweep's own limits persist: checking happens between events rather than during delivery, committed entries are compared by term at an index rather than full identity, and application is modelled by nextEnts on every step so the applied index never trails committed by more than one event.
limitations: Zero violations over 60 fixed seeds with 317 configuration events is not a rate bound and says nothing about seeds or event orders outside this set.

The harness registers a black-hole peer for the configured id, which is the repository's own test facility but not a real participant; a faithful configuration case needs a state machine that actually responds.
No requirement or comparison anchors were declared, so the receipt carries parsed events only and its meaning rests on this interpretation.

interpretations.rationale: Index 16 records the same four invariants with violations=0 while the configuration events now act on a participant that answers: 335 conf-change proposals were issued against 460 elections and 461 ordinary proposals, and the configured node is a real raft instance with its own storage that starts outside its own configuration (the state a joining node has before it applies the change that adds it) rather than the package's black-hole stepper. This directly retires the earlier counterevidence that configuration changes altered quorums without ever testing whether a freshly configured participant can process entries, since the leader's replication to node 4 now reaches a state machine that appends, acknowledges and can itself apply the conf change that adds it. The suspicion under test - a counterexample to at-most-one-leader-per-term, to committed (index, term) consistency, to committed-index monotonicity, or to applied <= committed once support is counted while the tracked configuration changes - still has no witness in this event set. Two scoping facts keep the result from being read as more than that: the changes remain single-node Changes on node 4, so the joint-consensus decision path (a majority in both halves of a joint quorum) is still unexercised, and restarts from persisted storage are absent, so nothing here tests the interaction between a configuration change and a node that comes back with a configuration reconstructed from storage rather than from the log.
counterevidence: The configured node is added and removed by single-change proposals only; no proposal entered a joint configuration, so quorum decisions that must satisfy two majorities simultaneously were not part of the event stream.

Node 4's own storage ConfState is pinned to voters {1,2,3}, so a restart of node 4 in this harness would rebuild it outside the configuration its log describes - a mismatch that is invisible here because no restart event exists.

The harness now points the network at node 4 directly rather than through newNetwork's peer constructor, whose branch installs all supplied peers as voters; the sweep therefore relies on the harness's own registration to model a non-member node, which is a harness property rather than something the target establishes.
limitations: Zero violations with 335 configuration events over 60 fixed seeds is not a rate bound and does not extend to other seeds or event orders.

Checks still happen between events rather than during message delivery, committed entries are compared by term at an index rather than full identity, and application is modelled by nextEnts on every step.
No requirement or comparison anchors were declared, so the receipt carries parsed events only and its meaning rests on this interpretation.

interpretations.rationale: Index 16 reports the four invariants with violations=0 while configuration events now include joint transitions: 356 conf-change proposals were issued against 468 elections and 460 ordinary proposals, and the runner log shows the joint configurations being entered and left (the harness only sets Transition=JointImplicit, so the leave proposals come from the target's own AutoLeave path in appliedTo, which advances only when the joint change has been applied). This closes the specific counterevidence the previous interpretation recorded - that no proposal had entered a joint configuration, so quorum decisions requiring a majority in both halves of a joint config were untested - since commit and vote tallies now run under (V0 && V1) configurations with the outgoing voters retained, and the suspicion's targeted mechanism (support counted while the tracked configuration changes) is exercised across a configuration transition rather than around one. The result remains a holds-only statement about this fixed event set: no witness appeared for at-most-one-leader-per-term, committed (index, term) consistency, committed-index monotonicity, or applied <= committed. Two things must not be read into it: the harness's event mix decides how often a joint config is entered and left, and a single seed set cannot bound a violation rate; and the configuration subject is still node 4 alone, which is added as learner or voter or removed, so promotion or demotion of an existing voter (a change to a member that is already serving) is still absent together with all restart events.
counterevidence: The joint transitions concern only node 4's membership, so a joint configuration that changes the status of an existing voter - the case where a serving member's own eligibility changes while it holds a log - was not exercised.

Restarts remain absent, so nothing here tests a node returning with a configuration reconstructed from storage rather than from the log it applied, which the earlier knowledge entry shows is the only configuration raft reads on restart.
The guard's liveness witness is still unmeasured: the sweep never records whether a configuration left a majority with committed-but-unapplied conf changes while no voter could campaign.
limitations: Zero violations with 356 configuration events over 60 fixed seeds, including joint transitions, is not a rate bound and does not extend to other seeds or event orders.
Checks still happen between events rather than during delivery, committed entries are compared by term at an index rather than full identity, and application is modelled by nextEnts on every step.

The harness registers node 4 directly with the network rather than through newNetwork's peer constructor, so modelling a non-member participant is a harness property, not something the target establishes.

interpretations.rationale: Index 16 shows the four invariants with violations=0 while 471 restart events ran alongside 249 configuration changes, 466 elections and 452 ordinary proposals. The restart event is the one that could plausibly produce a witness for committed-index regression, because it rebuilds a node from what an application would have persisted - hard state and last applied ConfState - and the check compares that node's committed index with the maximum it had previously reported; no such regression appeared, and neither did a committed (index, term) contradiction, two leaders in one term, or applied > committed. This retires the third item the previous interpretation listed as missing from the event set, and with it the earlier knowledge entry's premise that storage is the only configuration source on restart is exercised rather than only read: the harness supplies exactly that ConfState, and the rebuilt instance adopts it without a configuration-equivalence panic and without diverging from the cluster. The result stays a holds-only statement for this fixed event set, and two omissions must stay visible: the sweep still records no liveness witness for configurations left with committed-but-unapplied changes while no voter can campaign, and configuration events still only touch node 4, so demotion of an existing serving voter (which changes the status of a member that already holds a log) was not exercised.
counterevidence: A restart that is rebuilt and immediately re-registered can be caught up by the leader before the next check, so an interruption in the restarted node's own history may be invisible to a between-events check.
The harness supplies the ConfState itself, so the receipt tests that a restarted instance adopts a correct configuration, not that an application necessarily records one.
The absent liveness witness means the sweep cannot distinguish 'no safety violation' from 'no electable voter' in the states it passes through.
limitations: Zero violations with 471 restarts over 60 fixed seeds is not a rate bound and says nothing about other seeds, restart schedules or storage faults.
Storage faults are outside the event set: writes always succeed and the restarted node always sees exactly what was persisted at the restart event.
Checks still happen between events rather than during delivery, and committed entries are compared by term at an index rather than full identity.

interpretations.rationale: Index 16 reports the four invariants with violations=0 and, for the first time, the liveness witness: stalled_states=0 over 60 seeds x 60 steps with 249 configuration changes (half of them joint transitions with the target's own auto-leave), 471 node restarts, 466 elections and 452 ordinary proposals. The witness fires only when a node holds a committed-but-unapplied configuration change and no node is promotable, i.e. exactly the state in which the campaign admission guard could cost the cluster a leader; it never fired, so within this event set the guard's suppression did not coincide with a configuration that had no candidate able to campaign. That is the bounded-liveness statement the question asked for, and it is bounded in both directions: zero occurrences over a fixed seed set neither bounds a rate nor covers event orders outside it, and because the counter only totals occurrences, a non-zero future count would need per-occurrence operands (seed, step, node states) to be interpretable. Together with the earlier receipts this closes the gap's event-set items - simple and joint configuration changes, a real joining participant, and restarts that adopt the ConfState storage supplies - while the remaining shortfalls stay recorded: configuration changes never demote an existing serving voter, storage faults are outside the event set, and checks still happen between events rather than during delivery.

984747de5ed94b4ea8f6977b2a92808f-gap-2.explanation: With configuration changes (simple and joint via JointImplicit with the target's auto-leave), a real joining participant, and restarts that rebuild a node from the hard state and applied ConfState an application would persist, the sweep's four invariants held (violations=0) across 60 fixed seeds with 249 configuration events and 471 restarts (CheckRuns 2a3cfe42597e4c9f813117a4f06d4bf1, ccc93c67a2b54e7a874ab9bc7eedce9a, c6015a9dcbe94734bfc7089fff19e5c1), and the liveness witness added in this revision reported stalled_states=0 (CheckRun 35a6c1074291424686f0360747f6c268 index 16), i.e. no state in this event set combined a committed-but-unapplied configuration change with having no promotable node. The remainder stays open on purpose: demotion of an existing serving voter, storage faults, and per-occurrence witness operands were not exercised, and a zero count is not a bound.

counterevidence: The witness is evaluated only at the check point after each event, so a configuration that briefly had no promotable voter between two check points would not be counted.

Zero occurrences cannot distinguish 'the guard never had this cost' from 'the event mix rarely produces a majority with committed-but-unapplied configuration changes'; the sweep does not record how often the antecedent (unapplied change present at all) held.
Demotion of an existing serving voter is still absent, so the configuration path where a member's own eligibility changes while it holds a log was not part of the counts.
limitations: stalled_states=0 over 60 fixed seeds bounds nothing outside this seed set or event order.
The counter totals occurrences without operands, so it can only support the negative as scoped, not diagnose an occurrence.
Storage faults, delivery-time checks and full entry-identity comparisons remain outside the harness, as in the earlier revisions.

interpretations.rationale: Two halves of this investigation must now be separated. The safety half stands on index 16: across 60 fixed seeds with 249 configuration changes (half joint, with the target's own auto-leave), 471 restarts rebuilt from persisted hard state and applied ConfState, 466 elections and 452 ordinary proposals, none of the four violation events fired, so the suspicion of a counterexample to leadership uniqueness per term, committed (index, term) consistency, committed-index monotonicity or applied<=committed has no witness in this event set. The liveness half does not stand: the antecedent counter added afterwards reports unapplied_conf_change_states=0 for the same revision, because the sweep applies every node to its committed index on every step, so no check point ever presented the conjunction the witness counts. My earlier sentence that the guard's suppression never coincided with a configuration lacking a promotable node was therefore an artifact of the event mix, not an observation about the guard, and I withdraw it. What remains is a necessary gap rather than a defect: the guard's bounded-liveness cost can only be measured if application is allowed to fall behind (apply a subset of nodes, or skip the apply step for a chosen node for a while) so that a committed-but-unapplied configuration change coexists with the question of who can campaign. Until that event exists, the defect claim for this investigation is unresolved rather than refuted, and the four-invariant safety result stays scoped to the event set that produced it.

knowledge.assertion: no check point observes a committed-but-unapplied configuration change in the sweep as written, so the witness's zero count is uninformative

counterevidence: The safety half inherits every limitation already recorded: checks between events rather than during delivery, term comparison rather than full entry identity, no storage faults, and configuration changes that never demote an existing serving voter.
The liveness counters in this receipt cannot be used as evidence in either direction: stalled_states=0 is uninterpretable while unapplied_conf_change_states=0.
limitations: The measurement that would settle the liveness half needs an application-lag event; the harness revision that would provide it is not built yet.

The engineering of the lag event matters: applying a subset of nodes changes which node's configuration is stale, and the receipt would have to show the antecedent counter is non-zero before any stalled_states value means anything.

result.summary: Interpreted the first sweep receipt whose liveness counters are interpretable (CheckRun 0e5183701ac3447c8398f246b9103a04: completed, tests_passed, exit 0, 17 parsed observations, 0 parse errors). Indices 0-15 reproduce probes A-C; index 16 reports seeds=60, steps_per_seed=60, elections=470, ordinary proposals=461, conf_change_proposals=262, restarts=429, unapplied_conf_change_states=48, stalled_states=0, violations=0, and no liveness_witness event because the witness never fired. Since application lag was introduced (a randomly chosen node skips its apply step about one time in six), the antecedent now holds at 48 of 3600 check points, so the zero is informative for this event set: in every one of those 48 states at least one node remained promotable, meaning the campaign suppression never coincided with a configuration that had no candidate able to campaign - a real, if descriptive, answer to the bounded-liveness side of the guard. The safety half is unchanged and now carries lag too: no witness for at-most-one-leader-per-term, committed (index, term) consistency, committed-index monotonicity or applied <= committed across 262 configuration changes (half joint with the target's own auto-leave), 429 restarts rebuilt from persisted state, and ordinary traffic. I updated the gap answer to reflect the receipts now covering configuration changes, joint transitions, a real joining participant, restarts and application lag, while deliberately leaving it unresolved: 48 antecedent observations over one fixed seed set bound nothing outside it, the witness checks that some node is promotable rather than that a quorum of voters can campaign, lag was one-step and never combined with a partition of the lagging node, demotion of an existing serving voter remains absent from the event set, and checks still happen between events with term-level rather than full-identity comparison of committed entries.

interpretations.rationale: Source-only reading of the count-based read-only flow. Positive part: positions are monotonically increasing counts (never reused for a later batch), acks are maxima, and a released read carries the commit index recorded at admission, so a confirmed read cannot be justified by acknowledgements collected for an earlier request; the leader's own ack is the admission position, so a majority echo is still required for confirmation, and pendingReadIndexMessages are answered only after the leader commits in its term, which can only raise the emitted index. Unresolved part: the term-change path. reset() replaces r.readOnly with a fresh instance (unconfirmed reads and acks dropped) while r.readStates is untouched, and releasePendingReadIndexMessages only replies when committedEntryInCurrentTerm() holds. I have not yet observed whether a read admitted just before a term change is dropped silently (a lost completion under a legal trigger) or answered later; the snapshot's own TestReadOnlyDuplicateRequest covers only the duplicate-ctx/delayed-heartbeat case and asserts indices are not too small, not that every admitted request completes.
counterevidence: The repo's own read-index selections (TestReadOnlyOptionSafe/Lease/WithLearner/ForNewLeader/DuplicateRequest, TestRaftFreesReadOnlyMem) pass in native local feedback, and TestReadOnlyDuplicateRequest explicitly asserts no too-small read index under delayed duplicate requests plus a leader change, which weakens the stale-index side of the suspicion.
limitations: No retained execution receipt yet: the local test runs are construction feedback and cannot establish a formal conclusion.

Doc.go's Ready/Advance contract does not state that every admitted ReadIndex request must be answered, so a dropped request would have to be argued as a bounded-liveness consequence of an actual trigger rather than a contract violation.

interpretations.rationale: Source-only reading of the campaign admission guard. hasUnappliedConfChanges scans (applied, committed] with pagination and returns true on the first conf-change entry; hup() then refuses to campaign, and promotable() independently refuses while a snapshot is pending/unstable. The guard is consistent with doc.go's statement that configurations take effect when applied, and with applyConfChange/switchToConfig which only reconfigure on application, so a node that campaigns while lagging application would otherwise campaign with a stale voter set. What remains open is whether the guard is complete for the paths that can present a stale voter set (restore from snapshot with only ConfState initialized, bootstrap with applied<committed, an application that rejects a change by zeroing NodeId, and MsgTimeoutNow where the guard also suppresses a requested transfer), and whether the suppression can be permanent for an otherwise eligible voter.
limitations: No existing test references hasUnappliedConfChanges directly, so its behavior is currently only read from source; it must be probed with a real log/apply prefix rather than asserted.

interpretations.rationale: The suspicion had two branches: (i) the guard may be bypassed so a node campaigns with a stale voter set, and (ii) the guard may permanently block a legal campaign. Branch (i) is refuted by events 1 and 2: with has_unapplied=true and an already-promotable voter, both the MsgHup path and the MsgTimeoutNow path leave the node in StateFollower(term=1) with msgs=0, and the runner log shows the same suppression reason on both paths, so the transfer path reaches campaign() only through the same guard. The voter set used when campaigning is legitimate rather than stale: after the application catches up (event 3) the node reports has_unapplied=false and campaigns at term 2 with vote=1 and MsgVote addressed to voters [2,3], and event 0 records that this config (voters_before=[1,2,3]) is the applied configuration. Branch (ii) is refuted by the same event 3 plus the control at events 4-5: the block is transient, keyed on the entry type in (applied, committed] rather than on the applied/committed gap itself (the control has the identical gap and campaigns immediately). What remains is a bounded-liveness cost, not a safety defect: while the entry is unapplied the node cannot campaign and cannot take over a requested transfer, which is the documented intent that configurations take effect on application.

c6f44be10c0445b7a091b7db545cd614-gap-1.explanation: With a committed-but-unapplied conf change the node refrains from campaigning on both triggers (events 1-2: StateFollower, term 1, msgs=0; runner log 'cannot campaign at term 1 since there are still pending configuration changes to apply' on the MsgHup and MsgTimeoutNow paths), and a later campaign is possible once raft's applied index covers the entry (event 3: has_unapplied=false, StateCandidate at term 2, MsgVote to voters [2,3]; control events 4-5 show the effect is caused by the entry type, not by the applied/committed gap).

knowledge.assertion: hup() returns without campaigning when hasUnappliedConfChanges() is true, for both MsgHup and MsgTimeoutNow
campaign() addresses vote requests to the tracked voters of the current configuration, here [2,3]

counterevidence: The node is promotable=true throughout (events 0, 4), so the refusal does not come from promotable(); it is specifically hasUnappliedConfChanges, which strengthens the reading that the guard is the cause rather than an admission in promotable.

The post-apply campaign (event 3) carries vote targets [2,3] from the pre-change configuration because the harness only advanced raftLog.applied without calling ApplyConfChange; the voter set used in the probe is therefore the stored config, which is the config a leader would legitimately campaign with at that point.
limitations: The probe drives MsgHup/MsgTimeoutNow directly on a node whose storage prefix and Config.Applied are supplied, not a tick-driven election of a live cluster, so it establishes the guard's effect and its transience but not the wall-clock or tick cost of the suppression inside a running cluster.

The bounded-liveness cost for a requested transfer (leader keeps dropping proposals while leadTransferee != None) is visible in source but was not exercised by this harness; it is registered as investigation @transfer_stall.

interpretations.rationale: The question had two possible defect shapes: a stale (too small) read index, or a lost completion. Events 6-9 select the second and exclude the first for the exercised path. Event 7 shows the request admitted with unconfirmed_reads=1, read_states=0 and the admission commit index recorded as 2; event 8 shows that after the term change the node holds read_states=0, unconfirmed_reads=0, confirmed_reads=0 and ctx_A_completed=false, so the request is dropped, never emitted with a smaller index. Event 9 is the control that separates 'drops on term change' from 'read confirmation is broken': a read admitted on the new leader (commit_now=3, index_B=3) goes from read_states_before_ack=0 to read_states_after_ack=1 with ctx_B_completed=true as soon as one peer heartbeat response carrying the leader's context arrives, which is also the count-based confirmation the source predicted. A dropped completion is not a defect under the applicable contract: Node.ReadIndex documents that the request can be lost without notice and that ensuring read index retries is the user's job, so the caller duty is established by the target's own interface statement, and the exercised drop is exactly that documented lossiness rather than a wrong index being served.

c6f44be10c0445b7a091b7db545cd614-gap-0.explanation: The request is dropped, not answered stale: after admission with unconfirmed_reads=1 (event 7), the term change leaves read_states=0, unconfirmed_reads=0, confirmed_reads=0 and ctx_A_completed=false (event 8), so nothing is emitted for that context and no smaller index can be observed; the confirmation path itself still functions on the new leader (event 9: ctx_B_completed=true with index_B=3 equal to the commit index at admission), and the lossiness is the caller duty stated by Node.ReadIndex.

knowledge.assertion: a released ReadState is justified by a quorum of ack positions and carries the commit index recorded at admission

limitations: The probe steps MsgReadIndex directly into the leader rather than through Node.ReadIndex/RawNode.ReadIndex, so it shows the state-machine outcome and not the API-level return value or the Ready/ReadStates plumbing; the documented caller duty was read from node.go/doc.go rather than exercised.

Only one trigger of the term change was exercised (a higher-term campaign message from a peer); other authority losses that rebuild readOnly (for example a snapshot restore or a leadership transfer racing an admitted read) were not covered.
interpretations.joint_history: Same single invocation as the campaign-admission interpretation: CheckRun 238d3a23d8624c438b85ec18f90a7b2b is one execution of one fixed harness (fixed-experiments/075c21493fd94adc9bdc30a30b2cbff1-experiment/assurance_generated_test.go) containing both probes, so events 6-9 and events 0-5 come from the same process, the same fixed inputs and the same receipt, with no separate producer or intermediate history between them. The experiment record is attached to question-1 because the submission can carry only one experiment request; the receipt itself is shared, and its parsed indices 6-9 are the decisive operands for this question.

interpretations.rationale: The declared hypothesis was that the transfer neither completes nor deadlocks but is bounded by one election timeout, with proposals resuming afterwards and the transfer becoming possible once the transferee applies its committed configuration. The receipt confirms each leg in order. Event 10 establishes the prefix the claim needs: the leader is StateLeader(term 1, committed 2), the transferee is StateFollower with applied 0 and committed 2 and has_unapplied true, and the leader already has the transferee matched to its last index (r1_match_r2 2 == r1_last_index 2), which is exactly the condition under which the leader sends MsgTimeoutNow immediately. Event 11 shows the transfer is accepted as a pending duty (lead_transferee 2) while the transferee does not campaign (StateFollower, term 1), so the guard is what stops the handover rather than a transport or match problem. Event 12 shows the cost is real but scoped: a proposal during the window returns 'raft proposal dropped' (is_proposal_dropped true). Event 13 shows the bound: after the leader's electionTimeout ticks, lead_transferee is 0, the leader is still StateLeader(term 1) and a proposal is accepted again (proposal_err empty), i.e. abortLeaderTransfer released the pending duty within one election timeout instead of leaving it forever pending. Events 14-15 show the duty is transferable rather than lost: once the transferee's applied index reaches its committed index (has_unapplied false), the retried transfer completes with the transferee as StateLeader(term 2) and the former leader as StateFollower(term 2). A delayed transfer whose delay is caused by the transferee's own application lag, with the old leader still able to serve proposals after the abort, is not a defect under the stated conditions; the honest counterweight is that during the window the leader rejects client proposals, which is a client-visible cost of a request the application itself asked for, and the sweep of random configurations and authority changes remains to be done.

knowledge.assertion: hup() refuses to campaign on the leadership-transfer path reached via MsgTimeoutNow while hasUnappliedConfChanges() is true
campaign() addresses vote requests only to the tracked voters of the current configuration, as in the completed retry at term 2

counterevidence: Event 12 shows a proposal is rejected with ErrProposalDropped while the transfer is pending, so the bounded-liveness account must not be read as 'no cost': the cost is a proposal-rejection window whose length is determined by the transferee's application lag, and the receipt only measures it for one tick-driven abort (event 13) rather than for a live cluster's scheduling.

Events 10-15 exercise one configuration (three voters plus a staged learner) and one transfer target; nothing in the receipt constrains the same sequence during a joint configuration or when the transferee is the only node lagging while the rest are applied.
limitations: Application lag is modelled by not advancing raftLog.applied on the transferee; the receipt therefore shows the protocol's behavior given that lag, not how a real application creates it.
The abort was produced by ticking the leader through its own electionTimeout, so the bound observed is in protocol ticks under this harness's scheduling rather than wall-clock time.

The transfer completes in the receipt through the network's MsgTimeoutNow delivery on the retry; no independent completion path (for example a transfer while the leader is also being removed) was exercised.

interpretations.rationale: Index 16 reports the sweep's only output: 60 seeds times 60 steps produced 459 elections and 446 proposals with violations=0, and the event carries the note that absence of violations is a holds-only result for this event set rather than a safety proof. For the four invariants actually checked after every event - at most one leader per term, no index already known committed ever observed with a different term, per-node committed-index monotonicity, and applied <= committed - the receipt therefore contains no counterexample, which is consistent with the source-level explanation that commitment and leadership require quorum-intersecting support under the simple configuration used here (MajorityConfig.CommittedIndex/VoteResult with the joint min/majority semantics). The absence is nevertheless bounded by what the harness actually did: it emitted no violation event of any of the four kinds, and it also emitted no configuration-change or restart event, because the executed case omits both while the registered discriminator named them. I am recording that as a necessary gap and keeping the conclusion scoped to the exercised event set; the defect claim is refuted only in the narrow sense that this event set produced no witness for the suspicion, not because the invariants were established for the protocol.
counterevidence: The sweep's coverage is smaller than the discriminator promised: no ConfChange/ConfChangeV2 proposal, no joint or learner configuration and no restart from persisted storage appeared in the event stream, so the mechanism most likely to threaten the invariants (support counted under a configuration that changes while entries are unapplied) was not part of this receipt.

A zero-violation count over 60 seeds cannot bound the violation rate; it states only that no witness appeared in this fixed event set, and the harness checked committed terms only for indices the nodes actually reported as committed, so an entry committed by a majority but never observed at any checked node is invisible to it.
limitations: Invariant checking happens after each event, not during message delivery, so an intermediate inconsistency that is repaired before the next check point would not be observed.
The committed-entry check compares terms at an index rather than full entry identity, which is adequate for log-matching violations but does not by itself detect a same-term payload difference.
Application is modelled with nextEnts on every step, so the applied index is never more than one event behind committed; a real application's lag patterns are not represented.
No comparison or requirement anchors were declared for this case in the experiment request, so the receipt carries parsed events only and its meaning rests on this interpretation.

interpretations.rationale: Index 16 shows the sweep with configuration changes admitted into the event stream: 317 conf-change proposals were actually issued (against 452 ordinary proposals and 467 elections) and the four invariants still reported violations=0, so the receipt contains no witness for at-most-one-leader-per-term, committed (index, term) divergence, committed-index regression, or applied > committed once nodes apply committed conf changes through applyConfChange. This is the first receipt whose event set reaches the mechanism the suspicion named - support counted while the tracked configuration changes - because the earlier revision applied no configuration at all. The absence is still bounded: the changes are single-node Changes on node 4 only, so no joint configuration and no promotion/demotion of an existing voter was exercised, node 4 never responded (black-hole stepper) so every committed decision rested on the original three voters, and restarts from persisted storage are missing entirely. Two construction facts from this revision belong in the record: messages addressed to a configured-but-absent node crash the repository's network helper (raft_test.go:4117 dereferences a missing state machine), and only registering the package's own black-hole stepper for that id makes configuration events safe to run; consequently the receipt's configuration coverage is real but does not include a newly configured node that participates. The conclusion is therefore holds-only for this event set, with the defect claim refuted only in the narrow sense that no witness appeared.
counterevidence: Only single-node changes on node 4 were proposed, so the joint-consensus decision path (both halves of a joint quorum) was not part of the event stream even though the gap names it.
Node 4 never processed a message, so configuration changes altered quorums and progress tracking without ever testing whether a freshly added participant can vote, be promoted, or be snapshotted.

The sweep's own limits persist: checking happens between events rather than during delivery, committed entries are compared by term at an index rather than full identity, and application is modelled by nextEnts on every step so the applied index never trails committed by more than one event.
limitations: Zero violations over 60 fixed seeds with 317 configuration events is not a rate bound and says nothing about seeds or event orders outside this set.

The harness registers a black-hole peer for the configured id, which is the repository's own test facility but not a real participant; a faithful configuration case needs a state machine that actually responds.
No requirement or comparison anchors were declared, so the receipt carries parsed events only and its meaning rests on this interpretation.

interpretations.rationale: Index 16 records the same four invariants with violations=0 while the configuration events now act on a participant that answers: 335 conf-change proposals were issued against 460 elections and 461 ordinary proposals, and the configured node is a real raft instance with its own storage that starts outside its own configuration (the state a joining node has before it applies the change that adds it) rather than the package's black-hole stepper. This directly retires the earlier counterevidence that configuration changes altered quorums without ever testing whether a freshly configured participant can process entries, since the leader's replication to node 4 now reaches a state machine that appends, acknowledges and can itself apply the conf change that adds it. The suspicion under test - a counterexample to at-most-one-leader-per-term, to committed (index, term) consistency, to committed-index monotonicity, or to applied <= committed once support is counted while the tracked configuration changes - still has no witness in this event set. Two scoping facts keep the result from being read as more than that: the changes remain single-node Changes on node 4, so the joint-consensus decision path (a majority in both halves of a joint quorum) is still unexercised, and restarts from persisted storage are absent, so nothing here tests the interaction between a configuration change and a node that comes back with a configuration reconstructed from storage rather than from the log.
counterevidence: The configured node is added and removed by single-change proposals only; no proposal entered a joint configuration, so quorum decisions that must satisfy two majorities simultaneously were not part of the event stream.

Node 4's own storage ConfState is pinned to voters {1,2,3}, so a restart of node 4 in this harness would rebuild it outside the configuration its log describes - a mismatch that is invisible here because no restart event exists.

The harness now points the network at node 4 directly rather than through newNetwork's peer constructor, whose branch installs all supplied peers as voters; the sweep therefore relies on the harness's own registration to model a non-member node, which is a harness property rather than something the target establishes.
limitations: Zero violations with 335 configuration events over 60 fixed seeds is not a rate bound and does not extend to other seeds or event orders.

Checks still happen between events rather than during message delivery, committed entries are compared by term at an index rather than full identity, and application is modelled by nextEnts on every step.
No requirement or comparison anchors were declared, so the receipt carries parsed events only and its meaning rests on this interpretation.

interpretations.rationale: Index 16 reports the four invariants with violations=0 while configuration events now include joint transitions: 356 conf-change proposals were issued against 468 elections and 460 ordinary proposals, and the runner log shows the joint configurations being entered and left (the harness only sets Transition=JointImplicit, so the leave proposals come from the target's own AutoLeave path in appliedTo, which advances only when the joint change has been applied). This closes the specific counterevidence the previous interpretation recorded - that no proposal had entered a joint configuration, so quorum decisions requiring a majority in both halves of a joint config were untested - since commit and vote tallies now run under (V0 && V1) configurations with the outgoing voters retained, and the suspicion's targeted mechanism (support counted while the tracked configuration changes) is exercised across a configuration transition rather than around one. The result remains a holds-only statement about this fixed event set: no witness appeared for at-most-one-leader-per-term, committed (index, term) consistency, committed-index monotonicity, or applied <= committed. Two things must not be read into it: the harness's event mix decides how often a joint config is entered and left, and a single seed set cannot bound a violation rate; and the configuration subject is still node 4 alone, which is added as learner or voter or removed, so promotion or demotion of an existing voter (a change to a member that is already serving) is still absent together with all restart events.
counterevidence: The joint transitions concern only node 4's membership, so a joint configuration that changes the status of an existing voter - the case where a serving member's own eligibility changes while it holds a log - was not exercised.

Restarts remain absent, so nothing here tests a node returning with a configuration reconstructed from storage rather than from the log it applied, which the earlier knowledge entry shows is the only configuration raft reads on restart.
The guard's liveness witness is still unmeasured: the sweep never records whether a configuration left a majority with committed-but-unapplied conf changes while no voter could campaign.
limitations: Zero violations with 356 configuration events over 60 fixed seeds, including joint transitions, is not a rate bound and does not extend to other seeds or event orders.
Checks still happen between events rather than during delivery, committed entries are compared by term at an index rather than full identity, and application is modelled by nextEnts on every step.

The harness registers node 4 directly with the network rather than through newNetwork's peer constructor, so modelling a non-member participant is a harness property, not something the target establishes.

interpretations.rationale: Index 16 shows the four invariants with violations=0 while 471 restart events ran alongside 249 configuration changes, 466 elections and 452 ordinary proposals. The restart event is the one that could plausibly produce a witness for committed-index regression, because it rebuilds a node from what an application would have persisted - hard state and last applied ConfState - and the check compares that node's committed index with the maximum it had previously reported; no such regression appeared, and neither did a committed (index, term) contradiction, two leaders in one term, or applied > committed. This retires the third item the previous interpretation listed as missing from the event set, and with it the earlier knowledge entry's premise that storage is the only configuration source on restart is exercised rather than only read: the harness supplies exactly that ConfState, and the rebuilt instance adopts it without a configuration-equivalence panic and without diverging from the cluster. The result stays a holds-only statement for this fixed event set, and two omissions must stay visible: the sweep still records no liveness witness for configurations left with committed-but-unapplied changes while no voter can campaign, and configuration events still only touch node 4, so demotion of an existing serving voter (which changes the status of a member that already holds a log) was not exercised.
counterevidence: A restart that is rebuilt and immediately re-registered can be caught up by the leader before the next check, so an interruption in the restarted node's own history may be invisible to a between-events check.
The harness supplies the ConfState itself, so the receipt tests that a restarted instance adopts a correct configuration, not that an application necessarily records one.
The absent liveness witness means the sweep cannot distinguish 'no safety violation' from 'no electable voter' in the states it passes through.
limitations: Zero violations with 471 restarts over 60 fixed seeds is not a rate bound and says nothing about other seeds, restart schedules or storage faults.
Storage faults are outside the event set: writes always succeed and the restarted node always sees exactly what was persisted at the restart event.
Checks still happen between events rather than during delivery, and committed entries are compared by term at an index rather than full identity.

interpretations.rationale: Index 16 reports the four invariants with violations=0 and, for the first time, the liveness witness: stalled_states=0 over 60 seeds x 60 steps with 249 configuration changes (half of them joint transitions with the target's own auto-leave), 471 node restarts, 466 elections and 452 ordinary proposals. The witness fires only when a node holds a committed-but-unapplied configuration change and no node is promotable, i.e. exactly the state in which the campaign admission guard could cost the cluster a leader; it never fired, so within this event set the guard's suppression did not coincide with a configuration that had no candidate able to campaign. That is the bounded-liveness statement the question asked for, and it is bounded in both directions: zero occurrences over a fixed seed set neither bounds a rate nor covers event orders outside it, and because the counter only totals occurrences, a non-zero future count would need per-occurrence operands (seed, step, node states) to be interpretable. Together with the earlier receipts this closes the gap's event-set items - simple and joint configuration changes, a real joining participant, and restarts that adopt the ConfState storage supplies - while the remaining shortfalls stay recorded: configuration changes never demote an existing serving voter, storage faults are outside the event set, and checks still happen between events rather than during delivery.

984747de5ed94b4ea8f6977b2a92808f-gap-2.explanation: With configuration changes (simple and joint via JointImplicit with the target's auto-leave), a real joining participant, and restarts that rebuild a node from the hard state and applied ConfState an application would persist, the sweep's four invariants held (violations=0) across 60 fixed seeds with 249 configuration events and 471 restarts (CheckRuns 2a3cfe42597e4c9f813117a4f06d4bf1, ccc93c67a2b54e7a874ab9bc7eedce9a, c6015a9dcbe94734bfc7089fff19e5c1), and the liveness witness added in this revision reported stalled_states=0 (CheckRun 35a6c1074291424686f0360747f6c268 index 16), i.e. no state in this event set combined a committed-but-unapplied configuration change with having no promotable node. The remainder stays open on purpose: demotion of an existing serving voter, storage faults, and per-occurrence witness operands were not exercised, and a zero count is not a bound.

counterevidence: The witness is evaluated only at the check point after each event, so a configuration that briefly had no promotable voter between two check points would not be counted.

Zero occurrences cannot distinguish 'the guard never had this cost' from 'the event mix rarely produces a majority with committed-but-unapplied configuration changes'; the sweep does not record how often the antecedent (unapplied change present at all) held.
Demotion of an existing serving voter is still absent, so the configuration path where a member's own eligibility changes while it holds a log was not part of the counts.
limitations: stalled_states=0 over 60 fixed seeds bounds nothing outside this seed set or event order.
The counter totals occurrences without operands, so it can only support the negative as scoped, not diagnose an occurrence.
Storage faults, delivery-time checks and full entry-identity comparisons remain outside the harness, as in the earlier revisions.

interpretations.rationale: Two halves of this investigation must now be separated. The safety half stands on index 16: across 60 fixed seeds with 249 configuration changes (half joint, with the target's own auto-leave), 471 restarts rebuilt from persisted hard state and applied ConfState, 466 elections and 452 ordinary proposals, none of the four violation events fired, so the suspicion of a counterexample to leadership uniqueness per term, committed (index, term) consistency, committed-index monotonicity or applied<=committed has no witness in this event set. The liveness half does not stand: the antecedent counter added afterwards reports unapplied_conf_change_states=0 for the same revision, because the sweep applies every node to its committed index on every step, so no check point ever presented the conjunction the witness counts. My earlier sentence that the guard's suppression never coincided with a configuration lacking a promotable node was therefore an artifact of the event mix, not an observation about the guard, and I withdraw it. What remains is a necessary gap rather than a defect: the guard's bounded-liveness cost can only be measured if application is allowed to fall behind (apply a subset of nodes, or skip the apply step for a chosen node for a while) so that a committed-but-unapplied configuration change coexists with the question of who can campaign. Until that event exists, the defect claim for this investigation is unresolved rather than refuted, and the four-invariant safety result stays scoped to the event set that produced it.

knowledge.assertion: no check point observes a committed-but-unapplied configuration change in the sweep as written, so the witness's zero count is uninformative

counterevidence: The safety half inherits every limitation already recorded: checks between events rather than during delivery, term comparison rather than full entry identity, no storage faults, and configuration changes that never demote an existing serving voter.
The liveness counters in this receipt cannot be used as evidence in either direction: stalled_states=0 is uninterpretable while unapplied_conf_change_states=0.
limitations: The measurement that would settle the liveness half needs an application-lag event; the harness revision that would provide it is not built yet.

The engineering of the lag event matters: applying a subset of nodes changes which node's configuration is stale, and the receipt would have to show the antecedent counter is non-zero before any stalled_states value means anything.

interpretations.rationale: Index 16 gives the first sweep receipt in which the liveness witness has its antecedent and the safety counters are unchanged: application lag was introduced by skipping a randomly chosen node's apply step about one time in six, so 48 of the 3600 check points had at least one node holding a committed-but-unapplied configuration change, and in every one of those 48 states at least one node remained promotable - stalled_states=0 with no liveness_witness event emitted, since the witness only emits when the conjunction holds. That is a real, if descriptive, answer to the bounded-liveness question the guard raises: in this event set the campaign suppression never coincided with a configuration that had no candidate able to campaign, so the guard's cost never became a leaderless configuration here. The safety half is unchanged and now carries application lag as well: 262 configuration changes (half joint, with the target's own auto-leave), 429 restarts rebuilt from persisted state, 470 elections and 461 ordinary proposals produced violations=0, so no witness for at-most-one-leader-per-term, committed (index, term) consistency, committed-index monotonicity or applied<=committed. Both halves stay scoped: 48 antecedent observations over one fixed seed set bound nothing outside it, the witness is evaluated only at check points between events, and the event mix fixes how often lag and configuration changes overlap.

984747de5ed94b4ea8f6977b2a92808f-gap-2.explanation: The event-set items the gap named are covered by receipts: simple and joint configuration changes with the target's auto-leave and a real joining participant (CheckRuns 2a3cfe42597e4c9f813117a4f06d4bf1, ccc93c67a2b54e7a874ab9bc7eedce9a), restarts that rebuild a node from the persisted hard state and applied ConfState (c6015a9dcbe94734bfc7089fff19e5c1), and now application lag giving the liveness witness its antecedent (0e5183701ac3447c8398f246b9103a04 index 16: unapplied_conf_change_states=48, stalled_states=0). Within those event sets the four safety invariants held and the guard never left a configuration without a promotable node while a configuration change was pending.

knowledge.assertion: the witness's zero count is uninformative until the antecedent holds
application lag is what leaves a committed configuration change unapplied at a node

counterevidence: 48 antecedent observations out of 3600 check points is a thin sample for a liveness claim, and the sample is determined by the harness's own probability of skipping an apply step.
The witness checks promotability of any node, not whether a quorum of voters could actually campaign; a state where only a single node could campaign would still count as not stalled.
